lesson.title: Locating Points with Numbers
lesson.summary: Introduces the idea of a coordinate system as a way to turn "where something is" into numbers, using the rectangular (Cartesian) plane and polar coordinates as two ways of describing the same location.
lesson.body:
Before you can do any mathematics with shapes, motion, or change, you need a way to talk about *where* things are using numbers instead of pictures. That is the entire job of a coordinate system: it fixes a reference point and a set of directions, and then describes every other location by how far and which way it sits relative to that reference. Once location becomes numbers, you can add, compare, and calculate with it ,  which is why every later topic in this course, from graphing a function to measuring a rate of change, depends on having a coordinate system in place first.

The most familiar version is the rectangular, or Cartesian, coordinate system. You pick a fixed point called the origin, then draw two perpendicular number lines through it ,  a horizontal one (the x-axis) and a vertical one (the y-axis). Any point in the plane is then described by an ordered pair (x, y): x tells you how far to move left or right from the origin, and y tells you how far to move up or down after that. The reason this works is that once direction and distance along two independent axes are fixed, there is exactly one point that matches any given pair of numbers, and every point has exactly one such pair. That one-to-one matching between points and number pairs is the whole point of the system ,  it lets geometry become arithmetic.

But rectangular coordinates aren't the only valid way to pin down a location, because "how far right, how far up" is just one choice of reference directions. Polar coordinates instead describe a point by its straight-line distance from the origin, called r, and the angle, called θ, that the line to the point makes with a fixed reference direction (usually the positive x-axis). This is a completely different bookkeeping method for the same idea: instead of two perpendicular distances, you use one distance and one rotation.

To see that these two descriptions genuinely agree, take the point (3, 4) in rectangular coordinates ,  3 units right, 4 units up from the origin. Picture the right triangle formed by that horizontal leg of length 3, that vertical leg of length 4, and the straight segment connecting the origin to the point. By the Pythagorean theorem, the length of that segment is √(3² + 4²) = √25 = 5, so r = 5. The angle θ that segment makes with the x-axis satisfies tan(θ) = 4/3 (opposite over adjacent in that triangle), so θ = arctan(4/3). That means the same physical location can be written as (3, 4) in rectangular form or (5, arctan(4/3)) in polar form ,  two different number pairs describing one unchanged point in space.

The lesson to take from this isn't that one system is "correct" and the other a translation of it. Both are equally legitimate ways of assigning numbers to positions; the right-triangle relationship you just used is simply the bridge between them. Which system is more convenient depends on the problem: rectangular coordinates are natural when you're thinking in terms of horizontal and vertical movement, while polar coordinates are natural when a situation is organized around distance from a center and rotation, such as circular motion. As you go on to study graphs, functions, and later cylindrical and spherical coordinates for three-dimensional space, keep in mind that all of these are just different bookkeeping schemes built on the same core idea: fix a reference, then measure everything else relative to it.
